Deadly Lassa virus could be on the rise due to climate change










Copy link






Bookmark popover
Removed from bookmarks
Close popover








The natal multimammate mouse, a widespread African rodent and the main host of Lassa virus (Joachim Mariën/ Natural History Museum )


Increased rainfall driven by climate change could trigger more outbreaks of rodent-borne diseases such as Lassa fever, according to a study published in PNAS. 
Lassa fever causes an estimated 5,000 deaths annually in western Africa and is particularly dangerous in late-term pregnancies, causing fatal outcomes in over 80 per cent of cases. 
Researchers from the Natural History Museum and University of Oxford developed a predictive model using 30 years of rodent data that accurately matched human outbreak timings in Nigeria. 
Wetter weather boosts rodent populations by increasing food availability, while the Lassa virus survives between breeding seasons through high rates of mother-to-offspring transmission. 
Peaks in infected young rodents occur approximately one month prior to human outbreak peaks, offering potential for early warning systems to mitigate disease risk.

Andy Burnham is expected to unveil a new publicly owned company to invest in Britain’s electricity grid in his first Labour conference speech as Prime Minister in Liverpool on Tuesday afternoon.

Temperatures are set to rise to a balmy 26°C in parts of the UK today as the unusually hot spell continues into late September.



Southern areas are likely to see the highest temperatures, but the warmer weather is expected to be felt generally across the UK, with most places experiencing above-average temperatures for September.



This follows several months of heatwaves and drought conditions, and comes amid Met Office warnings of a “record-breaking” El Niño bringing wetter and stormier weather in the months ahead.

More than a hundred invasive species may colonise coastal waters worldwide by mid-century as sea levels rise due to climate change, a new study warns.
Invasive species like Chinese mitten crabs, Pacific oysters, and Asian tiger shrimps can lead to biodiversity loss and ecosystem change, with devastating economic impacts.
While previous studies have shown that climate change can alter species distributions on land and at sea, the impact of invasive, non-native marine species entering newly flooded areas due to the rise in sea levels has remained unclear.




“Sea-level rise may open new habitats for the landward expansion of marine non-native species into inundated coastal lands, which remains unexplored,” the latest study, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, explains. 
Estuaries are particularly vulnerable to invasive marine species, it notes, as they are hubs of human activity.






open image in gallery
European green crab (D. Hazerli)
The research models the future distribution of 122 non-native marine species, including the European green crab, the northern Pacific sea star, the bamboo worm and the pleated sea squirt under scenarios of continued sea-level rise. A scenario of moderate carbon emissions will see the global sea level rise by an average of 20cm by 2050.


In this scenario, the study predicts that between 290,000 and 470,000 sq km of inundated coastal land, almost the size of Italy, will become suitable habitat for invasive species, which often possess traits that give them competitive advantages over native species.
Invasive species like the Pacific oyster, the Atlantic blue crab, the predatory snail Veined rapa whelk, and the Asian tiger shrimp could colonise two-thirds of inundated coastal land in regions where they are already established.


Some of the marine creatures covered in the study, such as the striped barnacle, the orange-striped green sea anemone, the Indo-Pacific swimming crab, are expected to gain the most habitat from the inundated area. They are likely to spread most extensively in areas close to estuaries.

UN warns of ‘narrowing window’ to restore world’s forests


Food and Agriculture Organization urges governments to make forest restoration a national priority 




The world faces a “narrowing window” to restore forests essential for food security and resistance to the climate emergency, a United Nations report has warned.
More than 489m hectares (1.2bn acres) of forests have been cleared since 1990, while an even greater area is degraded, the world body said in a call for governments to make forest restoration a national priority.

The State of the World’s Forests report acknowledges recent steps forward in protection and tree planting around the globe but says action has not kept pace with commitments.
Over the past two decades, national, regional and global initiatives have promised to place more than 1bn hectares of land under restoration, but barely a fifth of that is actually being restored, the report by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) notes, saying: “Progress is uneven, and it is insufficient to meet growing global needs.”

Forests, which cover 4.14bn hectares (about a third of Earth’s land surface), store 714 gigatonnes of carbon and host up to 80% of the world’s terrestrial biodiversity. They also play an important role in regulating rainfall and in reducing hunger, with nearly one-third of the global population depending on them for livelihoods.


Threats are intensifying. Every year, about 127m hectares of forest are affected by fires, with further damage caused by insects, diseases and severe weather events. This is making forests ever more vulnerable, as it comes on top of pressure from farm expansion, the climate crisis, pollution and the extraction of fossil fuels and other resources.

“This widening gap between demand and sustainable supply highlights a structural imbalance that threatens both ecological integrity and the long-term viability of forest-based economies,” the report states.
It says remedial action on forests and other degraded ecosystems would benefit people, food security and the economy – with restoration of 1bn hectares estimated to generate $1.8tn in benefits each year.

articles.jina_text:
Londoners should brace themselves for icy weather and freezing temperatures as El Niño threatens to wreak havoc on weather once again this year. 




The weather phenomenon saw the capital face its hottest summer on record as wildfires and drought swept over the UK. 








But the worst could be yet to come with experts warning of a wet and stormy winter - and even a polar vortex - as the strongest El Niño event in 1,000 years develops over the Pacific Ocean. 


People shelter from the rain under an umbrella, in Westminster, central London (Jonathan Brady/PA)
PA Wire




It comes as government bodies and experts urge Britons to start stockpiling food and water in case of an emergency. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has advised that all homes should have cash, a supply of bottled water, and some tinned goods at their disposal should disaster strike, the Sun reported. 




El Niño is a naturally occurring climate cycle which takes place when sea temperatures become warmer than average, impacting air circulation patterns. This year’s El Niño has been dubbed “Godzilla” because of its exceptional impact and scale. 




As early as this week, rainy, gusty and stormy weather could blow over London and the UK. 




The Met Office has warned that there could be an increased likelihood of spells of rain and strong winds in comparison to average during parts of the season in London, but it is “not possible to attribute specific weather events to El Niño”. 




Meteorologists have also warned of a polar vortex - a large band of counter-clockwise winds that circle above the Earth’s North and South poles. 











The stratospheric polar vortex is not a weather system that moves into the UK, but changes in its strength could influence weather patterns lower down in the atmosphere, according to forecasters.




A spokesperson for the Met Office said: “A stronger-than-normal polar vortex can favour a stronger jet stream, which may increase the likelihood of mild, wet and windy conditions. 









“Conversely, a weaker polar vortex can sometimes increase the chances of colder weather affecting the UK.” 




Dan Holley, Met Office deputy chief forecaster, told the Independent that a “deep area of low pressure could pass close to the UK” this week.

Concern mounts over slow-moving, planetary-scale ‘Kelvin’ wave heading for California


The ocean phenomenon could raise sea levels by up to a foot as El Niño keeps warm water trapped along the coast




Concerns are mounting about an ocean phenomenon known as a Kelvin wave that could raise sea levels along the California coastline by up to a foot, as scientists say El Niño is supercharging the threat of storm surges and flooding in the coming months.
As an incredibly strong El Niño continues to develop in the Pacific, the phenomenon brings with it a strange shift in the ocean. The Kelvin wave phenomenon is created when trade winds that usually blow from South America towards Asia die down or reverse in El Niño years, setting off a massive, slow-moving slosh of water.

Kelvin waves are not like crashing waves at the beach. They are planetary in scale, spanning thousands of miles. And when a Kelvin wave kicks off, it brings with it an untold amount of warm water that slowly moves from the western Pacific, along the equator, towards South, Central and North America.


“You can follow them along … we see the higher sea levels along the equator, and when the wave reaches the coast of South America, it cannot continue to go eastward,” Severine Fournier, a research scientist studying ocean circulation at Nasa’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said. “So it goes north and south.”
One such wave hit the northern tip of South America in late August and has begun moving up towards the west coast of the US. That wave could reach California shores within days, and when it does, ocean scientists say it may raise sea levels by up to a foot for months as El Niño lingers and keeps that warm water trapped along the coast.
Nate Mantua, a research scientist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Southwest Fisheries Science Center, explained that in a typical year, there is a thick layer of warm water in the western Pacific.
“When the wind stops blowing or weakens, the force that’s holding that pile of water in place goes away, so that water surges or sloshes back towards California,” he said, noting researchers expect the influence of the Kelvin wave to linger through the winter and into early next year.
Mantua said Kelvin waves were a natural phenomenon that have been happening for thousands of years and measured by agencies like Noaa since record-keeping began. But sea levels have already risen about 8in over the last century, meaning Kelvin waves will add more water on top of a figure that’s already going up.


“We can predict a lot of the impacts,” he added, “but not all.”

An oil-like substance has been bubbling up in the River Avon in Bristol for years and killing wildlife, according to local residents who have made regular reports to the Environment Agency (EA).
Nicola Irvine, who lives in Crews Hole, said it had been like "pulling teeth" getting the EA to investigate the pollution since she contacted them in July 2025. 
Her partner, Toby White, said: "It's hard to describe how bad the smell is - at times it's like you're living on a petrol station and you start getting headaches."
The EA said it had already visited the site and was "continuing to investigate the source of contamination and its damage to the environment".
An EA spokesperson added: "While minor impacts have been found where the contamination has entered the watercourse, we have not found wider environmental effects downstream.
"We continue to work with landowners, the local authority and partner organisations to take action to protect the local environment."

Datacenter developers are manipulating the EPA’s air pollution permitting process to avoid emission controls and scrutiny of their projects, environmental advocates allege.

A month on from Nepal’s devastating floods, the disaster looks set to pile billions of pounds onto the country’s national debt burden – as experts warn it could become the latest country to face a huge debt bill from a climate crisis it has done little to cause.
On 26 August, more than 100 million cubic metres of rock and glacier broke away from Langtang Lirung mountain on Nepal’s northern border, triggering a 188km/h debris flood that buried villages, changed the course of rivers, and killed more than 1,400 people.
Scientists have since said that the event was made significantly more likely due to climate change, while the finance minister has warned that the final death toll could exclude that of a devastating 2015 earthquake. 




A subsequent rapid assessment of damage from the Nepali government has put the cost of recovery and reconstruction at $4.8 billion (£3.6bn) – equivalent to 11 per cent of the country’s GDP – and government figures have called for grant-based compensation as a matter of ‘climate justice’, given the fact that Nepal contributes to an estimated 0.1 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions each year. 





open image in gallery
Nepal suffered one of the worst catastrophes in its history when a tsunami-like flood cut a swathe of destruction claiming more than 1,400 lives and leaving 5,000 unaccounted for (AFP/Getty)
But the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage, established at the UN climate summit COP27 in Egypt in 2022, has so far secured just $822m in pledges, of which only $456m has actually been paid in, limiting the scale of support available to countries hit by disasters.

The fact that applications for withdrawals are limited to only $20m per country means the government will likely be forced to foot the bill with public debt, according to experts. 


“The loss and damage fund was created to support countries facing unprecedented climate disasters such as this, but it has nowhere near enough money,” says Ritu Bharadwaj, director of climate resilience at the International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED). 
“Even if - by a stroke of luck - they received the $20m they can apply for, that is less than half of a percent of the $4.8bn in damages.”


Bharadwaj continues: “Right now, there is still media attention. But once that goes, Nepal will be left to fend for itself - and that will mean borrowing huge amounts of money at an expensive rate, leaving the country at the mercy of creditors who can essentially use debt to control the country in an almost colonial manner.”

articles.title: Inside the new Labour row over Brexit
articles.raw_rss: Divisions in the party are rising over closer ties with Europe
articles.raw_content:
Labour has blocked a debate on whether to have closer ties with Europe at its annual conference next week as splits in the party widen over the scope of the Brexit reset.



The official reason for blocking the motion calling on the party to drop its blanket opposition to rejoining the single market, customs union or free movement of people is that it is not a “contemporary ” issue.



But insiders claim this party jargon really means the issue is “too sensitive”.





It comes as speculation increases over how far Andy Burnham will go in redrawing the UK’s relationship with Europe after he refused to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in the next Labour manifesto.



Overtures from Europe



The Government’s Brexit reset – which was on the verge of being signed by Sir Keir Starmer – is faltering amid a negotiating deadlock on a youth mobility or exchange scheme and UK demands that the UK should not be shut out of new “Made in Europe” laws.



These will dictate that public contracts within the EU favour companies based in the bloc. It is designed to counter cheap Chinese products, particularly clean technology and electric vehicles.



The debate was then turbocharged by former prime minister Sir Tony Blair, who called on his party to commit to rejoining within a decade. Unions earlier this month called on Labour to drop its red lines.



The i Paper also reported overtures from European Parliament Brexit chief Sandro Gozi for the UK to pursue a closer deal with the EU

articles.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
articles.raw_rss: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.
articles.raw_meta: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.
articles.jina_text:
The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.
They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.
But now, nearly all the snow is gone.
A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.
But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.
Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.









"There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".
She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.
Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history. 
Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.
But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.





Image caption, 

The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936



Proof of a warming planet




The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.
As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.
El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.
The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.
A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.
The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".

articles.jina_text:
Hurricanes Lala in August and Lowell in early September flooded homes and roads, downed trees and toppled electricity lines across the islands. Nolo, which strengthened to a hurricane on Thursday night, is expected to batter the islands with rain and high surf.

Despite its location, stretching across roughly 1,500 miles in the central north Pacific Ocean, Hawaii typically avoids the worst effects from hurricanes. In fact, the island chain so often dodges direct hits from the violent storms that it’s been quipped they have a force field around them.
But the islands have seen an unusual amount of severe storms this year. Already, more than 500 homes have been damaged or destroyed as Nolo threatens to unleash downpours that could measure in feet instead of inches.


“An event of this magnitude is somewhat rare,” Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said during a broadcast discussion as Lowell swirled closer last month, adding that Hawaii has not had a direct hurricane landfall since Iniki in 1992. That violent storm unleashed 145 mile-per-hour winds as it tore through Kauai, destroying or damaging roughly 70% of the island’s homes and businesses.


It’s not luck (or a force field) that typically protected the islands, but location, according to Dr Nicholas Grondin, assistant professor of environmental science at the University of Tampa. Among the most isolated chains of islands on Earth, Hawaii is simply a small target in the vast open ocean, Grondin explained in an editorial published by the Conversation.
Most approaching storms also must pass over cooler water temperatures to the east of the islands, which helps calm them. “Without warm oceans to provide fuel, hurricanes tend to weaken and fizzle out as they approach the islands,” Grondin said.
Sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific are, however, exceptionally warm this year due to El Niño. The climate phenomenon typically limits hurricane activity in the Atlantic and enhances the development and strength of storms in the Pacific. El Niño has already developed, but is expected to strengthen through the coming months, and forecasters have warned there is a high probability it will reach a historic intensity.
El Niño has caused hurricanes to form further to the south and west this year, according to Matthew Rosencrans, National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s lead forecaster for the seasonal hurricane outlook, which “puts them in a place where they could make that westward run towards the Hawaiian islands”.


It also makes for a lagging storm season. Hurricane risks typically extend from July to the end of November but fall off into the later months. September and October are far busier in El Niño years.
The climate crisis has also played a part in strengthening the storms. The effects of El Niño are layered on top of the warming trends.

A small uncrewed vessel has embarked on a lap around Antarctica and may not return for months.
The seven-metre craft, which looks like a large kayak in hi-vis orange, is expected to travel about 22,000km through inhospitable waters, propelled by powerful westerly winds and energy from the sun. The journey is seven times the distance between Sydney and Perth.

Along the way, it is expected to encounter massive waves, freezing temperatures, ferocious winds, and even the odd curious seal or albatross.
The mission? To collect data on carbon dioxide in the ocean and atmosphere, to help scientists better understand the role of ocean sinks.

Read more
Dr Elizabeth Shadwick, a principal research scientist at the CSIRO, said that after leaving Hobart the vessel would travel east towards New Zealand, “eventually scooching through the Drake Passage between the bottom of South America and Antarctica, then coming along past South Africa and back to us here, where we’ll pick it up.”
She hoped to see it again in seven to nine months.


View image in fullscreen
The vessel has a heavy keel to keep it upright and a solar sail to power it. Photograph: CSIRO AAPP
The autonomous vehicle made by the US maritime company Saildrone was designed to withstand the intrepid voyage, with a heavy keel keeping it upright, a rudder to steer and a fixed solar sail poking above the surface. It would be remotely monitored by the company, who would check in regularly via satellite, and, if necessary, nudge it in the right direction.


“It’s already been bashed around pretty heavily,” Shadwick said. “It’s quite a robust little device. We saw some eight metres of waves just the day after we deployed it and a 35-knot wind.”

articles.jina_text:
More tree planting, wetland restoration and drainage work could take place in parts of Northamptonshire to "safeguard nature for generations to come". 
West Northamptonshire Council has approved its first Local Nature Recovery Strategy (LNRS) which was required by the Environment Act 2021 and is the responsibility of all authorities.
It said the area was one of England's "most nature-depleted areas" and its wildlife sites "are often small, in poor condition, and isolated from one another".
Working with a range of partners the council hopes to improve landscapes that are "under unprecedented pressure" with some species in decline.
A spokesperson for the council said: "A healthy natural environment is essential for tackling climate change and wider environmental challenges. 
"The diversity of habitats and species provide essentials such as clean and plentiful water, food, clean air, productive soil, flood protection, shading and cooling, as well as benefits like space for recreation, exercise and wellbeing."
Nigel Stansfield, Reform UK's cabinet member for environment, recycling and waste, said: "Our aim is to safeguard nature for generations to come, and create cleaner, greener spaces that meet the needs of local communities and offer them an opportunity to connect with nature."
He said it was vital to have a workable strategy that sets out "how we intend to safeguard nature for generations to come."
Stansfield added he hoped the strategy would get organisations, landowners and local people to take action "to ensure our natural environment becomes more robust and resilient to provide the benefits we often take for granted".

“Gospić is our home,” Željka Šikić shouted to a crowd of 40,000 people outside the Croatian parliament earlier this month. The slogan is the name of a campaign she helped to set up to protest against the illegal dumping of waste in Gospić, a town in the mountainous Lika region of central Croatia.
Between 2022 and 2024, waste was illegally abandoned at several sites in the town. At one of the biggest, just 50 metres from Šikić’s home, an estimated 35,000 tonnes of waste, some of it hazardous, was dumped and buried.

In the dead of night, lorries heaving with waste would pass her front door and enter a nearby industrial site. This activity went largely unnoticed by the local authorities and police. But residents in Gospić were well aware and started taking it in turns to stay up to photograph the vehicles coming in and out of the site.
“I don’t think it should be our job to stay awake all night to see what’s going on,” Šikić says.


View image in fullscreen
An illegal waste site in Gospić in August. Photograph: Pixsell/Alamy
The waste became a blight on the community and a recent report from the Croatian Institute of Public Health revealed Pfas “forever chemicals” had been detected in groundwater samples nearby. Elevated concentrations of copper and lead were also detected in the soil.


Pfas are a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals that have been linked to serious health conditions, including several types of cancer. They are known as “forever chemicals” because of how long they persist in the environment.
Despite assurances that their drinking water is safe, a lack of trust means many residents have resorted to buying bottled water.
“I’m really scared,” Šikić says. “I would like to move house but I don’t know who would pay for the house on the first road next to the waste. I feel betrayed.”


View image in fullscreen
Residents took to filming lorries going in and out of one of the dumping sites on the outskirts of Gospić, seen here last month. Photograph: Pixsell/Alamy
In February 2025, years after the activity began, police and law enforcement officers arrested 13 people on suspicion of being part of the environmental criminal network involved in dumping the waste.
The main suspects, two Croatian nationals, were considered high-value targets by Europol and were believed to have orchestrated the illegal import of hazardous waste from Italy, Slovenia and Germany. It is thought the criminals generated upwards of €4m (£3.4m) in profit from this activity.


Waste crime is big business. Criminal networks often take advantage of the high costs associated with treating and disposing of waste properly. By falsifying documents to declare the waste as destined for recycling, they can save on the costs and pocket the difference.
Residents in Gospić had hoped the arrests would finally mean the site was shut down and cleaned up. But 18 months later, it is still there.

The UK faced its hottest summer on record this year, with much of the country experiencing drought and repeated heatwaves.
But temperatures and rainfall were not the same everywhere. Type in your postcode to see what summer 2026 was like in your area.



  
 
 
 
 
 
🏠🌤️ How was summer 2026 near you? 
A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive. 
As a result, we can't show information for your location, but data for the entire UK is available below.  
Data up to August 2026   
☀️ Temperature 
In the UK summer temperatures have been above average. 
The maximum daily temperature was 21.3C on average, which is 2.4C above what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. 
Virtually all of the UK experienced above average temperatures, driven by repeated heatwaves. 
Southern England and Wales saw heat far above usual. Temperatures were closer to normal across Scotland and Northern Ireland.

🌧️ Rainfall 
Rainfall in the UK has been below average this summer. 
Across the country a total of 195mm of rain fell on average, which is 23% below what it was for summer between 1991 and 2020. 
Summer months tend to be drier, but this year was exceptional. Only north-western Scotland saw more summer rain than usual, as droughts were declared across much of the rest of the UK. 
 
    
Total rainfall in summer 2026 as a percentage of 1991-2020 average summer rainfall  
 
Total rainfall map key 
 
Drier: brown 
Wetter: blue  
 
 
-100%: deepest brown 
No Change: white 
+100%: deepest blue          
About the data  
 
Where does the data come from? 
This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset     (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UK’s changing climate. 
The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically “fill in the gaps” between weather stations. 
The results displayed for each grid area represents a mean average of that grid cell and its nearest grid cells. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on the primary grid cell. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away.

A rare wildflower may have been wiped out in southern England after a summer of record heat and drought, conservationists have warned.




The field gentian, once widespread across Britain, was until recently so abundant in the New Forest in Hampshire that conservationists said counting the flowers was a challenge.








But after 2026 brought record warmth, successive heatwaves and severe drought — the third extreme summer in just five years — the plant may have disappeared from southern England altogether.




Experts described its possible disappearance as a “canary in the mine” for climate-driven species loss.




The Species Recovery Trust, a charity working to save some of Britain’s most endangered species, said the potential loss was “deeply worrying” because the field gentian had previously been abundant wherever it grew.


Dry and barren land in southern England following the summer's record-breaking heatwaves
The Species Recovery Trust/PA Wire




Dominic Price, director of the Species Recovery Trust, said the plant’s habitat — dry, “skeletal” grassland — was on the “absolute front line” of climate change.













“These habitats are becoming parched and dead in hot, dry weather,” he said.




The field gentian’s disappearance would be a striking example of how increasingly frequent heat and drought can push even locally abundant species towards extinction.




In 2022, when temperatures in the UK soared to 40C for the first time on record amid an extremely hot, dry summer, field gentian populations crashed for the first time across all known sites in the south of England, and went extinct at a county-level in Devon.









Populations recovered slightly the following year, and it was thought the New Forest populations could survive, due to their sheer size – often more than 5,000 plants at each site – and their ability for seeds to move with livestock into more sheltered areas.

The Species Recovery Trust has confirmed it has been unable to locate a single field gentian plant in the New Forest for the second year in a row.

Hundreds of thousands are expected to die, millions to go hungry. This is not just about weather patterns, but about injustice





Some warnings are so grave that it is almost impossible to fully comprehend them. They say that the weather pattern, which occurs roughly every two to seven years, may be the strongest in at least a millennium. articles.jina_text:
Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.

Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.


View image in fullscreen
The Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, visiting the Vantara zoo in Gujarat in March 2025. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”

“It was like the classic sound effect of a cricket in a film, a beeping sort of little trilling sound,” said Phelps, who works at Knepp Estate in West Sussex. Europe’s biggest economy, Germany, has committed to phasing out fossil fuels by 2045, despite fierce debate about its green policies.
In a roadmap published on Wednesday, the German government set out for the first time an explicit promise of “transitioning away” from fossil fuels. Previous pledges were only for “carbon neutrality”.

The plans include ramping up renewable energy from 55% to 80% of electricity generation by 2030, with an additional 12GW of onshore wind, and a target of 215GW of solar energy by 2030. The previously stated target of winding down coal use in the next decade, with a view to an exit from coal in 2038, was also reaffirmed, with the potential for an earlier target of 2035.
Emissions of methane, a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, will be cut by 30% by 2030, in accordance with a global methane pledge signed in 2021.


Andreas Sieber, head of global political strategy at 350.org, said the plan marked a “notable shift” in making the phaseout of fossil fuels an explicit policy goal. But he warned that Germany’s ministry for economic affairs and energy was also pushing intensely for greater use of gas.
“The economic ministry keeps sabotaging the transition away from fossil fuels,” he said. “This year has shown in the starkest terms that fossil-fuel dependence is a risk for everyone as it exposes households and businesses in Germany and around the world to price shocks, volatility and geopolitical insecurity.”
Germany’s former climate envoy Jennifer Morgan said the government must put more effort into electrifying transport and heating. “Accelerating the shift from coal, oil and gas to clean renewables will bolster energy independence and insulate consumers from price shocks at a critical moment,” she said. “However, a roadmap is only the starting line.”
She said the strategy must be paired with a faster, more deliberate rollout of green electrification.
The push for heat pumps to replace gas boilers came under attack from the far-right wing of German politics after a heating law was passed in 2023 that would have banned the installation of most oil and gas heating. Alternative für Deutschland made the issue a key campaigning point and forced a watering down of the rules earlier this year, while the party’s co-leader Alice Weidel has described wind turbines as “windmills of shame”. articles.jina_text:
The UK has been warned over ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month.
The UK was among countries facing downgraded growth forecasts in a report by the influential Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday.
That came as the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) told the BBC that Britain and the US needed to reduce debt due to spiralling borrowing costs.
The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war has pushed up the cost of crude oil leading to higher fuel and energy costs, which in turn has driven up inflation around the world.
The UK economy will grow by slightly less than expected next year, according to the OECD which now expects growth of 1% next year rather than 1.1%.
However, it said the UK had proved more resilient than expected this year, upgrading its forecast for growth 0.9% to 1.1%.
Meanwhile, IMF head Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC on Tuesday that global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost".
"[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.





















'Get on top of your debt issues' IMF boss tells governments
Inflation has also pushed up the cost of interest on government debt, which alongside an unexpected surge in government borrowing in August has added to the pressure on Healey.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has made easing the cost of living for households one of his key aims, while the government is under pressure to spend more on defence.
However, Burnham and Healey face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households while sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules. 
The impact of higher fuel prices next year depends on how long supply disruptions last, the OECD said. Stockpiles of oil and supplies from outside the Gulf states have helped cushion the effects on economies so far, it said.
Risks to the global economy include the war in the Middle East and climate-change related supply shocks, the OECD said.

Experts are predicting a wet and stormy autumn that could develop into an icy winter after the “super El Niño” smashed global benchmarks to become the strongest event in history.
The Met Office said the “unprecedented” phenomenon, which has already helped push temperatures to reach the hottest summer on record, will continue to have “far-reaching” implications for weather conditions across the world.

The “super” El Nino weather event and the record global heat it is driving could cause almost half a million additional deaths worldwide over the next six months, a new report has warned.
Researchers say that up to 451,000 extra heat-related deaths between June and the end of February could be linked to El Nino, compared with the number of heat deaths expected in a typical year. 
The report, published by the Climate Impact Lab based at the University of Chicagom, said the heaviest toll would fall on less affluent countries, which are already struggling with food insecurity and high energy costs, driven partly by climate change and the fallout of the Iran war.





The Sahel region of Africa, the semi-arid countries along the southern fringe of the Sahara Desert, is expected to be hit hardest, with about 66,800 additional deaths linked to the heat, the report found. 
Other major hotspots include South and Southeast Asia and parts of Latin America, with researchers projecting about 19,400 additional deaths across the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia, 19,300 in Indonesia, 15,800 in India and 13,300 in Brazil.

A generation of political leaders has failed to galvanize sufficient action on the climate crisis for so long now that it was perhaps little surprise that an audience in New York City turned to a three-and-a-half-year-old red furry monster for inspiration on Tuesday.
Elmo, the Sesame Street denizen, made a starry appearance at a Climate Week event that highlighted how the impacts of global heating affect children. The red creature, who frequently refers to himself in the third person, recounted to the audience his fear when a storm hit Sesame Street, an event depicted in a recent episode that featured the singer Post Malone.

“We all feel scared sometimes, but courage is when you feel scared but you still help others,” Elmo said at the event, which was named “Big Storms, Big Feelings”. “I tried to help others by giving lots of hugs and playing music on Elmo’s xylophone. Our message to global leaders: we need solar power everywhere by the decade’s end 





As climate experts from around the world gather in New York for their annual week of talking through the world’s deepest dilemma, the vibes are mostly bad.
Though 2026 seems likely to set a new global temperature record (and 2027, as El Niño gathers steam, is almost certain to break it), and though the planet has careened from one climate disaster to another (European heatwaves that killed tens of thousands, a Nepali flood that wiped out entire communities), and though scientists warn that we’re reaching precisely the global tipping points they’ve long feared (the new research on the faltering great currents of the Atlantic should send a literal chill up your spine), there’s a distinct lack of political momentum.

The host superpower is attacking country after country in search of oily “energy dominance”; even the noblest of its opponents (Canada’s Mark Carney, hope of democratic rebirth in the Americas) is busy building new oil and gas pipelines in the hopes it can bolster his besieged economy. Britain, which finally purged coal power from its energy system last year, now seems poised to start new drilling in the North Sea. If there’s an apocalyptic fear that can still rouse politicians to action, it seems to be AI agents breaking through firewalls, not European nations facing firestorms.


But there is one solitary (and very literal) ray of sunshine amidst this gloom: the steady rise of solar, wind and batteries. That clean energy trinity has broken out of its Chinese base and over the last few years expanded quickly across the planet – from Karachi to California to Cuba, solar panels are going up faster than any energy source has ever grown. It’s even begun to demonstrate that it can drive emissions down: China seems to have started on its downward slope years before most thought it could, and California has cut the use of gas to produce electricity in half in the world’s fourth-largest economy.

Small island nations have urged world leaders gathered in New York not to abandon efforts to limit global warming to 1.5C, warning that the goal remains a legal obligation rather than an aspiration.
The Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), a coalition of 39 small islands and low-lying coastal nations, said in a statement delivered at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday that "1.5°C is not an arbitrary goal that would be nice to achieve. It is the legally affirmed limit, endorsed by the UNGA, committed to by countries to protect people, ecosystems and economies".
The statement, delivered by Anne Rasmussen, Aosis's lead climate change negotiator, said the best available science showed that limiting the scale and duration of any overshoot of 1.5°C, and bringing warming back under that threshold, remained possible. 





"We absolutely cannot surrender our pursuit of 1.5°C," it said.
Ms Rasmussen said countries gathered for the assembly's 81st session needed to "treat escalating climate change impacts with the urgency this crisis merits", adding that "clear, concrete commitments must be set out to effectively respond to climate change and realign with 1.5°C."

articles.raw_content:
Nearly half a million people are projected to die in the next six months from soaring temperatures brought by the super El Niño, which has already reached record-breaking levels.



The climate phenomenon, which forms in the Pacific Ocean, is “firmly established and is expected to strengthen further” in the coming months before peaking at the end of the year, according to the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO).



Climate scientists now predict 451,000 people across the world will die due to additional heat. 



Professor Michael Greenstone, co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab which produced the report on additional deaths, said this is “such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbours, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives”.



The temperature rise in the Pacific Ocean where the El Niño forms has now reached 3.08°C, latest data shows. This is above the 3.02°C registered in November 2015 – the previous high in 150 years of records. The temperature is measured against the average of 1991-2020.





El Niño is part of a natural cycle, called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, and forms when warmer waters spread across the central and eastern Pacific Ocean. It is associated with widespread changes in the climate system that can last for up to a year.



The WMO said there was an “exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100 per cent” that this El Niño will last until February 2027.

Fears are mounting that the next UN secretary general will downgrade the priority of the climate crisis, according to climate and civil society experts.
The current secretary general, António Guterres, has been the most forthright on the subject, calling fossil fuel companies “the godfathers of climate chaos” and warning governments they are rushing down a “highway to hell” by failing to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

His repeated championing of the urgency of the crisis and willingness to take on vested interests are credited with significant global impacts, forcing governments to confront their policy failures and keeping alive the aims of the 2015 Paris climate agreement, despite the rising tide of populism and disinformation.
Guterres must step down at the end of his second five-year term on 31 December and the choice of his successor will be one of the top concerns among the scores of heads of government meeting in New York this week for the UN general assembly.
Many of Guterres’s most likely successors have shown less enthusiasm for tackling the climate crisis, despite rising alarm at its impacts, and experts have told the Guardian that some of the candidates could be “disastrous” yet could enjoy the support of influential countries including the US and its allies.

New report predicts a heavy toll from Nigeria to the US – and comes on top of existing impacts of the climate crisis




More than 450,000 people are projected to die from the additional heat brought by the super El Niño in the next six months, according to estimates by climate scientists.
The toll is on top of the early deaths resulting from temperatures already driven up by the climate crisis. It will strike across the globe, from Indonesia to India, and Nigeria to the US. Many further deaths are expected from the droughts, wildfires and flooding that El Niños bring.

The heat deaths have been estimated at regional level, and the researchers said the projections therefore identified where measures to protect people could be put in place and save lives. Such actions could include better heat forecasts, cooling centres where people can shelter, increased staffing for medical facilities at the hottest times and protections for outdoor workers.

The El Niño currently heating up the planet burst through the highest temperature ever recorded for the phenomenon on Monday, several months before its expected peak. The heat is so much greater than previous events that scientists have called it “mind-blowing” and “Godzilla-level”. El Niños are natural climate events but may be made worse by global heating.
“The estimate of 451,000 people is such a large number that it can be numbing, but it is made up of parents and children, grandparents and neighbours, people going to work, caring for families, and living their lives,” said Prof Michael Greenstone, co-founder of the Climate Impact Lab and at the University of Chicago, who co-authored the report.

Trump invades the UN with a brutish speech

Ted Widmer





Gone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years ahead





Expectations were low for Donald Trump’s address to the UN on Tuesday, and yet somehow it was even worse than expected. He does not perform well in formal settings, like chambers of government, preferring a blingier room, like Mar-a-Lago, or an outdoor rally. For years, he has made no secret of his hostility to the UN, and the very principles of international order that define it.
In recent years, that hostility has deepened into something more like a full-on assault, with frequent attacks on the international criminal court (perhaps out of fear that he will someday be indicted), on the UN’s climate agenda, and on Unesco (which the US decided to withdraw from in July 2025).

His flamboyant effort to launch a so-called Board of Peace in January (just before launching his war of choice on Iran) was another attack on the UN, which, at times, the president wondered if his new creation might simply replace.


Five months later, it has achieved little in the way of tangible results, except to demand huge sums of money from its small number of member nations, most of which are petrostates. Not one of those states can say that the Middle East is in better shape since the board came into existence, with a crisis that is deepening daily and may engulf Saudi Arabia soon.






Trump’s threat to annihilate Iran to UN general assembly is stunning, even for him

Read more
But even by Trumpian standards, this was a hollow speech, long on snarling belligerence and short on ideas or policy proposals. The president read robotically from a teleprompter for long stretches, except when he remembered one of the many complaints about the world that he has memorized from his rallies, and a history of grievances that goes back to his rise as a xenophobic developer in the 1980s.

Outgoing UN chief says polluters have treated atmosphere like an ‘open sewer’


António Guterres laments world leaders’ inaction and says oil and gas firms ‘must pay’ for climate devastation




For one last time, António Guterres tried to fix the world’s gaze upon the dangerously escalating climate crisis. But the departing UN secretary general found world leaders still largely focused on other issues, even after a painful summer of stunning climate-driven disasters.
Speaking to assembled dignitaries at the UN on Tuesday, Guterres railed against big oil for treating “the atmosphere as an open sewer” and warned again of the catastrophic effects of the climate crisis.

Guterres said: “Three years ago, in the mountains of Nepal, I sounded the alarm on accelerating glacier melt, warning that the rooftops of the world are caving in. Some dismissed it all as overstating dangers.
“But as tragic events have shown, impacts are arriving sooner, hitting harder, and spreading further than many anticipated.”
The UN chief said: “Those who polluted the most – and profited the most – must do far more to repair the damage they caused. Polluters must pay. And to the leaders, cities, civil society and citizens working to hold them accountable – you are on the right side of history. Keep going.”


View image in fullscreen
António Guterres at the UN in New York on Tuesday. Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/Shutterstock
Guterres has been an unflinching advocate for climate action in his nine years as UN secretary-general, and his departure from the role is set to leave a void in a geopolitical landscape consumed by wars, inflation fears and other economic concerns rather than our rapidly heating planet.


“António Guterres has been the most climate-forward secretary-general in UN history; and this speech shows why,” said Alden Meyer, a veteran climate policy expert at E3G. “He clearly laid out the stakes on the climate emergency – the horrific consequences of inaction and the tremendous opportunities in deploying the available solutions.”
This summer has been roiled by record heatwaves and wildfires across the US and Europe, as well as a catastrophic glacier collapse and landslide on the Nepal-Tibet border. A mounting El Nino event, perhaps the largest in modern human history, is meanwhile set to push global temperatures to new record highs and spur a spike in food insecurity.

The ministerial week of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) is meant to be the moment when the world comes together. Yet today fracture and fragmentation is dominant. Bad faith drives out good ideas. Hard power makes a mockery of international law. Even those with shared goals too often operate in silos. 
This dynamic is especially dangerous when the world is more connected than ever before. And it is more egregious when the world has more resources than ever before. We are witnessing a catastrophic collapse of global leadership at the exact moment humanity has all the risks of hyper-connectivity and all the potential of untold capital. 
My topic today addresses this dynamic. The twin and overlapping perils of war and climate change are breaking records. Yet political will, financial investment, and media attention have vanished.





When I was environment secretary in the UK twenty years ago, there was a fear that discussion of managing the effects of climate change (adaptation) meant going soft on preventing climate change (mitigation). But today, the failures and limits of mitigation mean we have no choice but to seek urgent mitigation and adaptation at the same time.
Adaptation means different things in different places.
This year there has been more coverage, MUCH more coverage, of the need for air conditioning in Europe than of the drought in Afghanistan, or desertification in the Sahel, or food insecurity in Somalia. For the next 25 minutes, I will turn the tables. More air conditioning is not the answer for the people who I want to place centre stage today.
